people.name: Anna
people.text: Working at home saves my daily journey, but I miss exchanging ideas without arranging a call. I work better when somebody can question my thinking immediately. One quiet day at home would be useful for reports; spending the entire week there would leave me feeling cut off. I would choose a mixture, with most days in the office.

people.name: Ben
people.text: I expected to enjoy the freedom, yet my workday has become longer. Messages arrive in the evening and I feel obliged to answer because my computer is always nearby. The lack of travel is helpful, but it has not compensated for losing a clear finishing time. I would return to the office if I could.

people.name: Cara
people.text: My job involves checking figures, so interruptions are costly. At home I can finish a difficult calculation before speaking to anyone. I was worried about feeling lonely, but regular calls have been enough. I deliberately shut down at five and leave the room. I see little reason to go back to our noisy office.

people.name: Dan
people.text: I manage a team whose work can mostly be done anywhere. Remote working could help colleagues with caring responsibilities, although some new staff still need face-to-face guidance. Before making it permanent, I would compare results over several months. A policy based only on whether people enjoy it would overlook the purpose of the business.

people.name: Anna
people.text: I use the bus every day and usually arrive on time. The fares are reasonable, especially with a monthly pass. My frustration is information: when something does go wrong, the app still shows the original timetable. Knowing whether a bus is actually coming would matter more to me than a small reduction in the price.

people.name: Ben
people.text: The railway is convenient for my office, but taking my children anywhere by train can cost more than driving. I understand that maintenance has to be paid for. Even so, family tickets ought to make occasional trips affordable. I would travel by rail much more at weekends if the total fare were less discouraging.

people.name: Cara
people.text: I used to think an extra bus route would persuade me to leave the car. Now that there is one near my house, I have discovered the real problem: it stops running before my evening shift ends. A service that cannot bring me home is only half a solution. Its frequency during the afternoon is already fine.

people.name: Dan
people.text: Although a new underground line would be impressive, improving existing buses should come first. Small changes to junctions could prevent delays and benefit many routes at once. Building the line might still make sense later, once those changes have been tried. Spending the whole budget on a single project now seems premature.

people.text: Recorded lessons fit around my changing work shifts. I often stop a video to try a calculation, then replay the explanation if I get stuck. people.text: I registered for an online course because the subject interested me. Without a fixed meeting time, however, I kept postponing the work. people.name: Anna
people.text: I enjoy finding out how ordinary people lived, rather than admiring famous possessions. A simple kitchen tool can interest me if its label explains what someone did with it. Digital screens sometimes help, but I would rather have a clear story than another button to press. The size of a collection is not what makes a visit memorable.

people.name: Ben
people.text: Taking my son to museums has changed what I look for. We need room to pause, sit down and talk about what we have seen. An exhibition can be fascinating and still feel exhausting if there is no place to rest. I am happy to pay for a visit that considers this; free admission alone does not persuade me.

people.text: I used to rush through every gallery to feel I had seen everything. Now I choose one section and spend an hour there. I sometimes return for another section, although travelling a long distance would make that approach less practical.

people.name: Dan
people.text: A museum should protect its objects, but that does not require visitors to remain passive. A good workshop lets people explore a technique without touching valuable originals. Such activities can make a difficult subject accessible. I support them as long as they explain the collection, rather than turning the museum into an unrelated entertainment centre.

people.name: Anna
people.text: The small shops near my home remember what I like and give useful advice. I cannot buy everything there, because their range is limited. For specialist items I still order online. Supporting local businesses matters to me, but pretending they can meet every need would not help them understand what customers actually want.

people.name: Ben
people.text: I used to buy groceries online to save time. After several deliveries with unwanted replacements, I began visiting a shop again. Choosing the food myself takes longer but avoids surprises when I cook. I might use delivery during a particularly busy week, provided I could reject substitutions before the order arrived.

people.name: Cara

Asking residents to change their habits without offering realistic access seems unfair. Lower prices would be welcome, but they would not solve my problem.

people.name: Dan
people.text: I run a bookshop and know that we cannot match every online discount. Instead, we organise events and help readers discover unfamiliar writers. These services take time, so I hope visitors who enjoy them will occasionally buy a book. I am not asking people to avoid the internet; I want them to recognise what their spending supports.

people.name: Anna
people.text: I train with friends twice a week. On days when I feel tired, knowing they are waiting gets me out of the house. The exercise itself would be much the same alone, but I doubt I would do it regularly. We do not compete over speed; keeping the appointment is more useful to me than improving a personal record.

people.name: Ben
people.text: The gym has everything I need, yet getting there uses time I cannot spare. Short sessions at home have been easier to maintain. I miss some equipment, but an ideal workout that never happens is less useful than a simple one I actually do. I would reconsider the gym if one opened closer to work.

people.name: Cara
people.text: Walking used to seem too gentle to count as exercise. Since I started climbing the hill near my flat, I have changed my mind. The effort is real, and being outdoors helps me relax afterwards. I am less interested in measuring steps than in how I feel. Bad weather occasionally keeps me in, but that is a small drawback.

people.name: Dan
people.text: After an injury I had to stop following the routine I found online. A professional helped me adapt it to what my body could manage. General advice can encourage people to start, but it should not replace individual guidance when something hurts. My progress is slower now, although I am more confident that it will last.

people.name: Anna
people.text: I book accommodation well ahead because arriving somewhere without a bed would worry me. Once that is settled, I leave the days open. A timetable of attractions makes a holiday feel like work. I might reserve a particularly popular museum, but I prefer discovering most things as I go along.

people.name: Ben
people.text: Last year I tried choosing restaurants and activities at the last moment. We wasted hours comparing options and disagreed about what to do. This year everyone will suggest a few priorities before we leave. I do not want a minute-by-minute plan, just enough agreement to avoid spending our holiday making the same decisions repeatedly.

people.name: Cara
people.text: A tour made me nervous because I assumed it would be rigid. In fact, our guide changed the schedule when the weather turned bad and offered different walks for different abilities. That flexibility persuaded me to book another. I would not choose any organised trip automatically, though; the group size and approach still matter.

people.name: Dan
people.text: Travelling outside the main holiday season often makes places quieter and more affordable. I enjoy that, but people should check what remains open. An empty beach is attractive; arriving to find every café closed is less convenient. I recommend the quieter months to independent travellers who are comfortable making a few compromises.

people.name: Anna
people.text: I check several reports when a story is important. Small differences in the facts can show what still needs confirming. This takes longer than reading a headline, but I would rather wait than repeat something misleading. For ordinary local events one reliable source is usually enough; I do not compare everything.

people.name: Ben
people.text: Constant news alerts made it difficult to concentrate. I now read a summary once in the evening and have switched off most notifications. I am still interested in events, but knowing about each development immediately rarely changes what I can do. An urgent local warning is the exception, so I keep those alerts enabled.

people.name: Cara
people.text: I like podcasts because an interview can reveal how a decision was reached. Hearing the reasoning matters more than simply learning the outcome. However, a confident voice can sound convincing without providing evidence. I look for programmes that challenge their guests and publish links, rather than ones that merely offer a pleasant conversation.

people.name: Dan
people.text: My students often share news through short social-media clips. Banning those platforms would probably make them ignore my advice. Instead, I ask them to trace a claim back to its original source. Clips can introduce a useful issue, but understanding what has been left out requires reading beyond them.

people.name: Anna
people.text: I follow recipes closely when making a dish for the first time. Once I understand the method, I adjust flavours to suit the people eating it. Experimenting before I know the basics tends to waste ingredients. The recipe gives me a dependable starting point rather than a rule I must follow forever.

people.name: Ben
people.text: My parents cooked without measuring much, so I assumed everyone could learn by watching. Trying to bake alone showed me otherwise: small changes in amounts affected the result. I now weigh ingredients carefully for cakes, although I still make soup by taste. Precision matters for some tasks more than for others.

people.name: Cara
people.text: A cookery class taught useful techniques, but the equipment was very different from my tiny kitchen. I struggled to repeat the dishes at home. What helped was choosing recipes using the tools I already had. I might take another class if it focused on everyday cooking in ordinary homes rather than professional facilities.

people.name: Dan
people.text: I cook with my teenage daughter on Sundays. Finishing dinner takes longer than doing it myself, and the kitchen is rarely tidy. Nevertheless, she is becoming confident about preparing food independently. I judge the session by what she learns, not by whether we produce a perfect meal at exactly the planned time.

people.name: Anna
people.text: The park near my home is most valuable as a quiet place to sit. I am not opposed to events, but holding them every weekend would remove that benefit. A few each summer could help fund maintenance. The council should decide how often to hold them by considering regular users as well as ticket buyers.

people.name: Ben
people.text: An unused area behind our school could become a garden. Some people want expensive landscaping immediately, but I favour starting with a few beds cared for by pupils. If interest continues, we can expand. A modest project that people maintain seems more promising than a beautiful space they soon neglect.

people.name: Cara
people.text: I support protecting local wildlife, yet closing every path through the woods could weaken that support. People care more about places they can experience. Marked routes away from sensitive areas would allow access while reducing disturbance. Restrictions during the nesting season may still be necessary, provided their purpose is explained.

people.name: Dan
people.text: Volunteers do excellent work cleaning the riverbank, but they should not be expected to replace proper rubbish collection. Without regular council support, the same waste soon returns. Community action can draw attention to the issue and improve things temporarily. A lasting solution also requires the public services to fulfil their responsibilities.
